commands.name: critical-analysis

commands.name: data-analysis

commands.name: grant-writing

commands.name: hypothesis-generation

commands.name: design

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx

This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. # Planning: The Synthetic Data Ceiling

Written before any experiment was run (pre-registration). Deviations are logged at the end.

## Situation note (resources)

The resource-finder stage was skipped for this run (`.neurico/pipeline_state.json` → `"skipped": true`):
there is no `literature_review.md`, `resources.md`, `papers/`, `datasets/` or `code/`. I gathered datasets
myself. In addition, `OPENROUTER_KEY` (and every other provider key) is **not set** in this environment,
so API models are unavailable. This study needs gradient-based training on synthetic data anyway, so all
models are real open-weight models run locally on the 4× RTX A6000.

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
Model-generated data is now the default way to stretch a small real dataset (distillation, augmentation,
instruction tuning). Practitioners must choose *how much* to generate, and the cost is linear in that
choice. If benefit saturates early, most generation budgets are wasted; if large ratios actively hurt,
they are harmful. A measured dose–response curve per task family is directly actionable.

### Gap in Existing Work
(From my own knowledge of the literature; no review file was supplied.)
- *Model-collapse* work (Shumailov et al. 2023/2024; Alemohammad et al. 2023 "MAD"; Dohmatob et al. 2024;
  Gerstgrasser et al. 2024; Bertrand et al. 2024) studies **recursive, multi-generation** self-training,
  and mostly reports perplexity or image quality. It says little about the **single-generation**
  augmentation setting people actually use, with a stronger teacher and a fixed real set.
- *Synthetic augmentation* work (He et al. 2022; Azizi et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2023 for images; ZeroGen,
  Yu et al. 2023, Li et al. 2023 for text classification) reports scaling curves for one task family at a
  time, with different generators, students, and metrics, so cross-domain comparisons are not possible.
- Nobody (to my knowledge) has run one protocol — same teacher, same student, same real-set size, same
  ratio grid — across code, reasoning, and creative generation, with a **real-data scaling control**
  and a direct **measurement of generator diversity saturation** as the proposed mechanism.

### Our Novel Contribution
A controlled dose–response study of the synthetic:real ratio (0 → 50:1) across three task families with a
shared protocol, explicit tests of the functional form (log vs. saturating vs. power-law), the "80% at
3:1" claim, the ">10:1 plateau/degradation" claim, and the cross-domain ordering, plus a mechanism check
(does effective sample diversity of the synthetic pool saturate?).

### Experiment Justification
- **E1 – Ratio sweep (core).** Fine-tune the student on 100 real + r·100 synthetic examples for each r in
  the grid, 3 tasks, 3 seeds. Gives the dose–response curve everything else depends on.
- **E2 – Real-data scaling control.** Same total sizes but all-real data. Without it a plateau cannot be
  attributed to *synthetic* data (it could just be student capacity / data saturation).
- **E3 – Pool diversity vs. pool size.** Tests the hypothesised mechanism (mode collapse): duplicates,
  distinct n-grams, embedding-space effective sample size of synthetic vs. real sets of equal size.
- **E4 – Zero-shot student baseline.** Anchors the scale: how much does any fine-tuning buy?
- **E5 (if time) – Ablations.** Unfiltered code synthetic data (removes the execution-verification
  advantage code enjoys), and a judge/quality view of creative outputs.

## Research Question
When a fixed real training set is augmented with data generated by a stronger model, how does held-out
performance on real data change with the synthetic:real ratio r, and does this differ between code
generation, mathematical reasoning, and creative writing?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- **H1a (shape):** gain(r) is better described by a·ln(1+r) than by linear, power-law, or bounded
  saturating forms.
- **H1b (80% @ 3:1):** [perf(3) − perf(0)] / [max_r perf(r) − perf(0)] ≥ 0.8.
- **H2a (plateau/degrade >10:1):** perf(50) ≤ perf(10) (within noise or lower); slope of perf on ln r for
  r ≥ 10 is ≤ 0.
- **H2b (mechanism):** the synthetic pool's diversity saturates (rising duplicate / near-duplicate rate,
  sub-linear distinct n-gram growth relative to real data) and this tracks the plateau.
- **H3 (ordering):** code is most resilient (latest peak, smallest drop at high r); creative degrades
  earliest (earliest peak / largest drop).

Independent variables: ratio r ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50}; task ∈ {code, math, creative};
data source ∈ {synthetic, real control}. Dependent variables below.

## Proposed Methodology

### Approach
Teacher → synthetic pool → student fine-tuning → evaluation on **real** held-out data.
- **Teacher/generator:** `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` (vLLM, T=1.0, top-p=0.95). Each generation request
  shows 3 random examples from that seed's 100 real examples and asks for one new example. The generator
  therefore only "knows" the task through the real seed set — the realistic augmentation setting.
- **Student:** `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, full fine-tuning (fp32 weights, bf16 autocast), AdamW,
  lr 2e-5, batch 16, 10% warm-up + cosine. Steps = max(3 epochs, 100 steps). Validation loss on a small
  **real** validation set is evaluated 8 times; the best checkpoint is used for testing (early stopping),
  so small-data conditions are not penalised by over- or under-training.
- A 14× teacher/student size gap makes this a distillation-style setting where synthetic data can help.

### Tasks and data
| Domain | Dataset (real) | Real seed set | Val | Test | Task metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code | MBPP (`full`) | 100 of 374 train | 90 (validation split) | 500 (test split) | pass@1, greedy |
| Math | GSM8K | 100 of train | 200 of train | 1319 (test split) | exact-match accuracy, greedy |
| Creative | ROCStories 2018 (human-written, title → 5-sentence story) | 100 of train | 200 | 1000 (NLL) / 500 titles (generation) | human-text perplexity; Fréchet embedding distance; diversity |

A metric common to all three domains: **per-token NLL of the real held-out reference answers**.
Each seed uses a different 100-example real set **and its own independently generated pool**, so seed
variance includes real-set and generator variance. Subsets are nested (r=1 ⊂ r=2 ⊂ …) to reduce noise
along a curve. Synthetic pools are *not* de-duplicated (duplication is part of the phenomenon). Code
samples are kept only if the teacher's solution passes the teacher's own asserts (standard practice;
flagged as an asymmetry and ablated in E5).

### Experimental Steps
1. Build splits; sanity-check formats; zero-shot student baseline (E4).
2. Generate pools (5,000 usable examples per task × seed; more if throughput allows).
3. Pilot one small and one large condition to verify the training/eval pipeline end to end.
4. E1 ratio sweep; E2 real control (GSM8K, ROCStories at all matched sizes; MBPP only to 374 = r≈2.7,
   limited by the dataset).
5. E3 diversity analysis; curve fitting and statistics; figures; report.

### Baselines
Zero-shot student; real-only (r=0); all-real at matched size (upper reference); teacher's own task score
where cheap to obtain.

### Evaluation Metrics
- Code: pass@1 on MBPP test (execution of the 3 hidden asserts; prompt shows the asserts as is standard).
- Math: accuracy of the number after `####`.
- Creative: perplexity of human test stories (primary, standard in the collapse literature); Fréchet
  distance between MiniLM embeddings of student stories and human stories for the same titles;
  distinct-n and mean pairwise embedding similarity of student stories (sampled at T=1).
- Normalised benefit B(r) = [perf(r) − perf(0)] / [max_r perf(r) − perf(0)], per task.

### Statistical Analysis Plan
- Curve fits on gain vs. r (all seed-level points): linear, a·ln(1+r), power law a·r^b, hyperbolic
  a·r/(r+k), exponential saturation a(1−e^(−r/k)); compare with AICc and R².
- H1b: point estimate of B(3) with a bootstrap CI (resampling seeds and test items).
- H2a: paired differences perf(50) − perf(10) and perf(50) − perf(peak) (paired by seed and test item;
  bootstrap CI / McNemar for binary metrics); OLS slope of perf on ln r for r ≥ 10.
- H3: compare tasks on r* (ratio achieving ≥95% of max benefit), B(3), and relative change from r=10 to 50.
- α = 0.05; three task families × a few planned contrasts → Holm correction within each hypothesis.
- With 3 seeds the between-seed CI is coarse; item-level paired tests provide the power, seed-level
  spread is shown in every plot.

## Expected Outcomes
Supports H: concave gains, B(3) ≥ 0.8 in all tasks, flat/negative slope after 10:1, rising duplicate rate,
code flattest at high r and creative turning down first. Refutes H: gains still rising at 50:1 (no
ceiling in range), B(3) well below 0.8, bounded-saturating or power-law clearly better than log, no
diversity saturation, or a different task ordering.

## Timeline and Milestones
Setup+plan 30 min → generation 30–40 min → sweep ~90 min (4 GPUs) → analysis 30 min → report 30 min.
Buffer ≈ 25%. Critical path: generation throughput, then the sweep.

## Potential Challenges
- Disk: `/data` has ~4 GB free → symlinked venv, no checkpoints saved, compressed outputs.
- Small effect vs. noise on MBPP (500 items) → paired item-level tests, nested subsets.
- Early stopping on real-val NLL may not select the best task-metric checkpoint → also log final-step NLL.
- Creative "performance" has no single accepted metric → report several and state which is primary.
- One teacher, one student, one real-set size → external validity limit; stated in the report.

## Success Criteria
A complete ratio × task × seed grid with real controls, statistical tests for each sub-hypothesis, and an
honest verdict (supported / partially / refuted) per sub-hypothesis.

# Planning: The Synthetic Data Ceiling

Written before any experiment was run (pre-registration). Deviations are logged at the end.

## Situation note (resources)

The resource-finder stage was skipped for this run (`.neurico/pipeline_state.json` → `"skipped": true`):
there is no `literature_review.md`, `resources.md`, `papers/`, `datasets/` or `code/`. I gathered datasets
myself. In addition, `OPENROUTER_KEY` (and every other provider key) is **not set** in this environment,
so API models are unavailable. This study needs gradient-based training on synthetic data anyway, so all
models are real open-weight models run locally on the 4× RTX A6000.

## Motivation & Novelty Assessment

### Why This Research Matters
Model-generated data is now the default way to stretch a small real dataset (distillation, augmentation,
instruction tuning). Practitioners must choose *how much* to generate, and the cost is linear in that
choice. If benefit saturates early, most generation budgets are wasted; if large ratios actively hurt,
they are harmful. A measured dose–response curve per task family is directly actionable.

### Gap in Existing Work
(From my own knowledge of the literature; no review file was supplied.)
- *Model-collapse* work (Shumailov et al. 2023/2024; Alemohammad et al. 2023 "MAD"; Dohmatob et al. 2024;
  Gerstgrasser et al. 2024; Bertrand et al. 2024) studies **recursive, multi-generation** self-training,
  and mostly reports perplexity or image quality. It says little about the **single-generation**
  augmentation setting people actually use, with a stronger teacher and a fixed real set.
- *Synthetic augmentation* work (He et al. 2022; Azizi et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2023 for images; ZeroGen,
  Yu et al. 2023, Li et al. 2023 for text classification) reports scaling curves for one task family at a
  time, with different generators, students, and metrics, so cross-domain comparisons are not possible.
- Nobody (to my knowledge) has run one protocol — same teacher, same student, same real-set size, same
  ratio grid — across code, reasoning, and creative generation, with a **real-data scaling control**
  and a direct **measurement of generator diversity saturation** as the proposed mechanism.

### Our Novel Contribution
A controlled dose–response study of the synthetic:real ratio (0 → 50:1) across three task families with a
shared protocol, explicit tests of the functional form (log vs. saturating vs. power-law), the "80% at
3:1" claim, the ">10:1 plateau/degradation" claim, and the cross-domain ordering, plus a mechanism check
(does effective sample diversity of the synthetic pool saturate?).

### Experiment Justification
- **E1 – Ratio sweep (core).** Fine-tune the student on 100 real + r·100 synthetic examples for each r in
  the grid, 3 tasks, 3 seeds. Gives the dose–response curve everything else depends on.
- **E2 – Real-data scaling control.** Same total sizes but all-real data. Without it a plateau cannot be
  attributed to *synthetic* data (it could just be student capacity / data saturation).
- **E3 – Pool diversity vs. pool size.** Tests the hypothesised mechanism (mode collapse): duplicates,
  distinct n-grams, embedding-space effective sample size of synthetic vs. real sets of equal size.
- **E4 – Zero-shot student baseline.** Anchors the scale: how much does any fine-tuning buy?
- **E5 (if time) – Ablations.** Unfiltered code synthetic data (removes the execution-verification
  advantage code enjoys), and a judge/quality view of creative outputs.

## Research Question
When a fixed real training set is augmented with data generated by a stronger model, how does held-out
performance on real data change with the synthetic:real ratio r, and does this differ between code
generation, mathematical reasoning, and creative writing?

## Hypothesis Decomposition
- **H1a (shape):** gain(r) is better described by a·ln(1+r) than by linear, power-law, or bounded
  saturating forms.
- **H1b (80% @ 3:1):** [perf(3) − perf(0)] / [max_r perf(r) − perf(0)] ≥ 0.8.
- **H2a (plateau/degrade >10:1):** perf(50) ≤ perf(10) (within noise or lower); slope of perf on ln r for
  r ≥ 10 is ≤ 0.
- **H2b (mechanism):** the synthetic pool's diversity saturates (rising duplicate / near-duplicate rate,
  sub-linear distinct n-gram growth relative to real data) and this tracks the plateau.
- **H3 (ordering):** code is most resilient (latest peak, smallest drop at high r); creative degrades
  earliest (earliest peak / largest drop).

Independent variables: ratio r ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50}; task ∈ {code, math, creative};
data source ∈ {synthetic, real control}. Dependent variables below.

## Proposed Methodology

### Approach
Teacher → synthetic pool → student fine-tuning → evaluation on **real** held-out data.
- **Teacher/generator:** `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` (vLLM, T=1.0, top-p=0.95). Each generation request
  shows 3 random examples from that seed's 100 real examples and asks for one new example. The generator
  therefore only "knows" the task through the real seed set — the realistic augmentation setting.
- **Student:** `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, full fine-tuning (fp32 weights, bf16 autocast), AdamW,
  lr 2e-5, batch 16, 10% warm-up + cosine. Steps = max(3 epochs, 100 steps). Validation loss on a small
  **real** validation set is evaluated 8 times; the best checkpoint is used for testing (early stopping),
  so small-data conditions are not penalised by over- or under-training.
- A 14× teacher/student size gap makes this a distillation-style setting where synthetic data can help.

### Tasks and data
| Domain | Dataset (real) | Real seed set | Val | Test | Task metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code | MBPP (`full`) | 100 of 374 train | 90 (validation split) | 500 (test split) | pass@1, greedy |
| Math | GSM8K | 100 of train | 200 of train | 1319 (test split) | exact-match accuracy, greedy |
| Creative | ROCStories 2018 (human-written, title → 5-sentence story) | 100 of train | 200 | 1000 (NLL) / 500 titles (generation) | human-text perplexity; Fréchet embedding distance; diversity |

A metric common to all three domains: **per-token NLL of the real held-out reference answers**.
Each seed uses a different 100-example real set **and its own independently generated pool**, so seed
variance includes real-set and generator variance. Subsets are nested (r=1 ⊂ r=2 ⊂ …) to reduce noise
along a curve. Synthetic pools are *not* de-duplicated (duplication is part of the phenomenon). Code
samples are kept only if the teacher's solution passes the teacher's own asserts (standard practice;
flagged as an asymmetry and ablated in E5).

### Experimental Steps
1. Build splits; sanity-check formats; zero-shot student baseline (E4).
2. Generate pools (5,000 usable examples per task × seed; more if throughput allows).
3. Pilot one small and one large condition to verify the training/eval pipeline end to end.
4. E1 ratio sweep; E2 real control (GSM8K, ROCStories at all matched sizes; MBPP only to 374 = r≈2.7,
   limited by the dataset).
5. E3 diversity analysis; curve fitting and statistics; figures; report.

### Baselines
Zero-shot student; real-only (r=0); all-real at matched size (upper reference); teacher's own task score
where cheap to obtain.

### Evaluation Metrics
- Code: pass@1 on MBPP test (execution of the 3 hidden asserts; prompt shows the asserts as is standard).
- Math: accuracy of the number after `####`.
- Creative: perplexity of human test stories (primary, standard in the collapse literature); Fréchet
  distance between MiniLM embeddings of student stories and human stories for the same titles;
  distinct-n and mean pairwise embedding similarity of student stories (sampled at T=1).
- Normalised benefit B(r) = [perf(r) − perf(0)] / [max_r perf(r) − perf(0)], per task.

### Statistical Analysis Plan
- Curve fits on gain vs. r (all seed-level points): linear, a·ln(1+r), power law a·r^b, hyperbolic
  a·r/(r+k), exponential saturation a(1−e^(−r/k)); compare with AICc and R².
- H1b: point estimate of B(3) with a bootstrap CI (resampling seeds and test items).
- H2a: paired differences perf(50) − perf(10) and perf(50) − perf(peak) (paired by seed and test item;
  bootstrap CI / McNemar for binary metrics); OLS slope of perf on ln r for r ≥ 10.
- H3: compare tasks on r* (ratio achieving ≥95% of max benefit), B(3), and relative change from r=10 to 50.
- α = 0.05; three task families × a few planned contrasts → Holm correction within each hypothesis.
- With 3 seeds the between-seed CI is coarse; item-level paired tests provide the power, seed-level
  spread is shown in every plot.

## Expected Outcomes
Supports H: concave gains, B(3) ≥ 0.8 in all tasks, flat/negative slope after 10:1, rising duplicate rate,
code flattest at high r and creative turning down first. Refutes H: gains still rising at 50:1 (no
ceiling in range), B(3) well below 0.8, bounded-saturating or power-law clearly better than log, no
diversity saturation, or a different task ordering.

## Timeline and Milestones
Setup+plan 30 min → generation 30–40 min → sweep ~90 min (4 GPUs) → analysis 30 min → report 30 min.
Buffer ≈ 25%. Critical path: generation throughput, then the sweep.

## Potential Challenges
- Disk: `/data` has ~4 GB free → symlinked venv, no checkpoints saved, compressed outputs.
- Small effect vs. noise on MBPP (500 items) → paired item-level tests, nested subsets.
- Early stopping on real-val NLL may not select the best task-metric checkpoint → also log final-step NLL.
- Creative "performance" has no single accepted metric → report several and state which is primary.
- One teacher, one student, one real-set size → external validity limit; stated in the report.

## Success Criteria
A complete ratio × task × seed grid with real controls, statistical tests for each sub-hypothesis, and an
honest verdict (supported / partially / refuted) per sub-hypothesis.

"""Execute model-written Python against assert-style tests in isolated subprocesses.

Each program runs in its own interpreter (`python -I`), in an empty temporary directory, with CPU-time
and memory limits and a wall-clock timeout. This is the usual HumanEval/MBPP-style harness, not a
security sandbox.
"""
import re
import resource
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

TIMEOUT_S = 10


def extract_code(text: str) -> str:
    """Take the first fenced code block if present, else the raw text."""
    m = re.search(r"```(?:python|py)?\s*\n(.*?)```", text, flags=re.S)
    if m:
        return m.group(1).strip()
    m = re.search(r"```(?:python|py)?\s*\n(.*)", text, flags=re.S)   # unterminated block (truncation)
    return (m.group(1) if m else text).strip()


def _limits():
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CPU, (TIMEOUT_S, TIMEOUT_S))
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (4 << 30, 4 << 30))
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_FSIZE, (1 << 20, 1 << 20))


def run_program(program: str) -> str:
    """Return 'pass', 'timeout', or the exception class name / 'error'."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        try:
            p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-I", "-c", program], cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True,
                               timeout=TIMEOUT_S, preexec_fn=_limits, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            return "timeout"
    if p.returncode == 0:
        return "pass"
    last = [l for l in p.stderr.strip().splitlines() if l.strip()]
    m = re.match(r"(\w+(?:Error|Exception))", last[-1]) if last else None
    return m.group(1) if m else ("timeout" if p.returncode in (-9, -24) else "error")


def check_many(codes: list, tests: list, setups: list = None, workers: int = 12) -> list:
    """codes[i] is run followed by tests[i] (list of assert strings). Returns a status string per item."""
    setups = setups or [""] * len(codes)
    progs = [f"{s}\n{c}\n\n" + "\n".join(t) + "\n" for c, t, s in zip(codes, tests, setups)]
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(workers) as ex:
        return list(ex.map(run_program, progs))

"""Generate synthetic training pools with the teacher model (vLLM offline inference).

Usage: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=g python src/generate_synth.py --jobs mbpp:0,gsm8k:0 --n_requests 6000

Request i of (task, seed) is fully determined by (task, seed, i): its 3 few-shot examples are drawn from
that seed's 100 real examples with an RNG keyed on (task, seed, i) and the sampling seed is derived from
the same key, so pools are resumable and extendable (re-running with a larger --n_requests appends).
"""
import argparse
import json
import random
import re
import time

import common as C
from exec_eval import check_many, extract_code

K_SHOT = 3
TEMPERATURE, TOP_P, MAX_TOKENS = 1.0, 0.95, 512

SYSTEM = "You are a careful dataset author who writes new training examples for an existing dataset."

INSTR = {
    "mbpp": ("Below are {k} examples from a dataset of short Python programming tasks.\n\n{shots}\n"
             "Write ONE new example for this dataset: a different programming task of similar style and "
             "difficulty, a correct solution, and exactly three assert-based tests that the solution passes. "
             "Use exactly this format and output nothing else:\n\n"
             "Task: <one-sentence task description>\nCode:\n```python\n<solution>\n```\nTests:\n```python\n"
             "<assert 1>\n<assert 2>\n<assert 3>\n```"),
    "gsm8k": ("Below are {k} examples from a dataset of grade-school math word problems.\n\n{shots}\n"
              "Write ONE new example for this dataset: a different word problem of similar style and "
              "difficulty with a correct step-by-step solution. The last line of the solution must be "
              "'#### <final numeric answer>'. Use exactly this format and output nothing else:\n\n"
              "Question: <problem>\nSolution: <step-by-step solution>\n#### <answer>"),
    "roc": ("Below are {k} examples from a dataset of five-sentence everyday short stories written by "
            "people.\n\n{shots}\n"
            "Write ONE new example for this dataset: a different story with a new title, in the same style, "
            "exactly five sentences long. Use exactly this format and output nothing else:\n\n"
            "Title: <title>\nStory: <five-sentence story>"),
}


def render_shot(task: str, ex: dict, i: int) -> str:
    if task == "mbpp":
        return (f"Example {i}:\nTask: {ex['text']}\nCode:\n```python\n{ex['code']}\n```\nTests:\n```python\n"
                + "\n".join(ex["tests"]) + "\n```\n")
    if task == "gsm8k":
        return f"Example {i}:\nQuestion: {ex['question']}\nSolution: {ex['answer']}\n"
    return f"Example {i}:\nTitle: {ex['title']}\nStory: {ex['story']}\n"


def build_prompt(task: str, seed_set: list, seed: int, req: int) -> str:
    rng = random.Random(f"{task}-{seed}-{req}")
    shots = rng.sample(seed_set, K_SHOT)
    return INSTR[task].format(k=K_SHOT, shots="\n".join(render_shot(task, s, i + 1) for i, s in enumerate(shots)))


def parse(task: str, text: str):
    """Parse a teacher completion into a unified example, or None if the format is violated."""
    text = text.strip()
    if task == "mbpp":
        m = re.search(r"Task:\s*(.+?)\s*Code:\s*```(?:python)?\s*\n(.*?)```\s*Tests:\s*```(?:python)?\s*\n(.*?)```",
                      text, flags=re.S)
        if not m:
            return None
        desc, code = m.group(1).strip(), C.clean_code(m.group(2))
        tests = [l.strip() for l in m.group(3).splitlines() if l.strip().startswith("assert")]
        if not desc or not code or len(tests) < 1:
            return None
        tests = tests[:3]
        return {"prompt": C.mbpp_prompt(desc, tests), "answer": C.mbpp_answer(code), "text": desc,
                "code": code, "tests": tests}
    if task == "gsm8k":
        m = re.search(r"Question:\s*(.+?)\s*Solution:\s*(.+)", text, flags=re.S)
        if not m or "####" not in m.group(2):
            return None
        q, sol = m.group(1).strip(), m.group(2).strip()
        sol = sol[: sol.rfind("####")] + "#### " + sol.split("####")[-1].strip().splitlines()[0].strip()
        gold = C.gsm_extract(sol)
        if not q or gold is None:
            return None
        return {"prompt": q, "answer": sol, "question": q, "gold": gold}
    m = re.search(r"Title:\s*(.+?)\s*\n\s*Story:\s*(.+)", text, flags=re.S)
    if not m:
        return None
    title, story = m.group(1).strip(), " ".join(m.group(2).split())
    if not title or len(story.split()) < 10:
        return None
    return {"prompt": C.roc_prompt(title), "answer": story, "title": title, "story": story}


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--jobs", required=True, help="comma list of task:seed")
    ap.add_argument("--n_requests", type=str, required=True, help="int, or task=int,task=int")
    ap.add_argument("--chunk", type=int, default=2000)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    n_req = ({k: int(v) for k, v in (kv.split("=") for kv in args.n_requests.split(","))}
             if "=" in args.n_requests else None)

    from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
    llm = LLM(C.TEACHER, dtype="bfloat16", max_model_len=3072, gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, seed=0)
    tok = llm.get_tokenizer()
    C.POOL_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    for job in args.jobs.split(","):
        task, seed = job.split(":")
        seed = int(seed)
        total = n_req[task] if n_req else int(args.n_requests)
        seed_set = C.real_seed_set(task, seed)
        path = C.pool_path(task, seed)
        done = {json.loads(l)["req"] for l in open(path)} if path.exists() else set()
        todo = [i for i in range(total) if i not in done]
        print(f"[{job}] {len(done)} done, {len(todo)} to generate", flush=True)
        for s in range(0, len(todo), args.chunk):
            reqs = todo[s:s + args.chunk]
            t0 = time.time()
            prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template(
                [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                 {"role": "user", "content": build_prompt(task, seed_set, seed, i)}],
                tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for i in reqs]
            sps = [SamplingParams(temperature=TEMPERATURE, top_p=TOP_P, max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS,
                                  seed=(hash((task, seed)) % 1000) * 1_000_000 + i) for i in reqs]
            outs = llm.generate(prompts, sps, use_tqdm=False)
            rows, n_tok = [], 0
            for i, o in zip(reqs, outs):
                txt = o.outputs[0].text
                n_tok += len(o.outputs[0].token_ids)
                ex = parse(task, txt)
                rows.append({"req": i, "parsed": ex is not None, "valid": ex is not None,
                             **(ex or {"raw": txt[:600]})})
            if task == "mbpp":   # execution filter: solution must pass the teacher's own tests
                idx = [k for k, r in enumerate(rows) if r["parsed"]]
                status = check_many([rows[k]["code"] for k in idx], [rows[k]["tests"] for k in idx])
                for k, st in zip(idx, status):
                    rows[k]["exec"] = st
                    rows[k]["valid"] = st == "pass"
            with open(path, "a") as f:
                for r in rows:
                    f.write(json.dumps(r) + "\n")

              "difficulty with a correct step-by-step solution. The last line of the solution must be "
              "'#### <final numeric answer>'. Use exactly this format and output nothing else:\n\n"
              "Question: <problem>\nSolution: <step-by-step solution>\n#### <answer>"),
    "roc": ("Below are {k} examples from a dataset of five-sentence everyday short stories written by "
            "people.\n\n{shots}\n"

        return f"Example {i}:\nQuestion: {ex['question']}\nSolution: {ex['answer']}\n"

"""Fine-tune the student on one training-set condition and evaluate it on real held-out data.

A worker processes every job whose index satisfies idx % n_workers == worker, skipping finished ones
(results/runs.jsonl is append-only, so the sweep is resumable).

    CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 python src/train_eval.py --worker 0 --n_workers 6 [--filter REGEX]

No checkpoints are written to disk (the best-validation weights are held in GPU memory).
"""
import argparse
import gzip
import json
import math
import random
import re
import time

import numpy as np
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

import common as C
from exec_eval import check_many, extract_code

LR, BATCH, EPOCHS, MIN_STEPS, N_VAL_EVALS = 2e-5, 16, 3, 100, 8
WARMUP_FRAC, WEIGHT_DECAY, MAX_LEN, GRAD_CLIP = 0.1, 0.01, 640, 1.0
GEN_BATCH = 160
REAL_CONTROL = {"gsm8k": [1, 3, 10, 50], "roc": [1, 3, 10, 50], "mbpp": [1, 2.74]}   # 2.74 -> all 374 MBPP train


def job_key(j):
    return f"{j['task']}|{j['cond']}|{j['ratio']}|{j['seed']}"


def all_jobs():
    jobs = [{"task": t, "cond": "zeroshot", "ratio": 0, "seed": 0} for t in C.TASKS]
    for t in C.TASKS:
        for s in C.SEEDS:
            jobs += [{"task": t, "cond": "synth", "ratio": r, "seed": s} for r in C.RATIOS]
            jobs += [{"task": t, "cond": "real", "ratio": r, "seed": s} for r in REAL_CONTROL[t]]
            if t == "mbpp":   # ablation E5: no execution filter on synthetic code
                jobs += [{"task": t, "cond": "synth_unfiltered", "ratio": r, "seed": s} for r in (3, 10, 50)]
    # biggest first, so interleaved assignment balances load across workers
    jobs.sort(key=lambda j: -j["ratio"] if j["cond"] != "zeroshot" else 1)
    return jobs


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- tokenisation
def encode(tok, ex):
    """Return (input_ids, labels) with the loss restricted to the assistant turn."""
    prefix = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": ex["prompt"]}], tokenize=False,
                                     add_generation_prompt=True)
    p = tok(prefix, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
    a = tok(ex["answer"] + "<|im_end|>", add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
    if len(p) + len(a) > MAX_LEN:
        a = a[:max(MAX_LEN - len(p), 8)]
    return p + a, [-100] * len(p) + a


def collate(items, pad_id):
    n = max(len(i[0]) for i in items)
    ids = torch.full((len(items), n), pad_id, dtype=torch.long)
    lab = torch.full((len(items), n), -100, dtype=torch.long)
    att = torch.zeros((len(items), n), dtype=torch.long)
    for k, (x, y) in enumerate(items):
        ids[k, :len(x)] = torch.tensor(x)
        lab[k, :len(y)] = torch.tensor(y)
        att[k, :len(x)] = 1
    return ids, att, lab


def batches(enc, rng):
    """Shuffled batches with light length-bucketing (less padding, same expected gradient)."""
    idx = list(range(len(enc)))
    rng.shuffle(idx)
    out = []
    for s in range(0, len(idx), BATCH * 32):
        chunk = sorted(idx[s:s + BATCH * 32], key=lambda i: len(enc[i][0]))
        out += [chunk[b:b + BATCH] for b in range(0, len(chunk), BATCH)]
    rng.shuffle(out)
    return out


@torch.no_grad()
def nll_per_item(model, enc, pad_id, bs=64):
    """Summed NLL and token count of the reference answer for every item."""
    model.eval()
    order = sorted(range(len(enc)), key=lambda i: len(enc[i][0]))
    sums, cnts = np.zeros(len(enc)), np.zeros(len(enc))
    for s in range(0, len(order), bs):
        ii = order[s:s + bs]
        ids, att, lab = (t.cuda() for t in collate([enc[i] for i in ii], pad_id))
        with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            logits = model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att).logits
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1].float().transpose(1, 2), lab[:, 1:],
                                                 ignore_index=-100, reduction="none")
        sums[ii] = loss.sum(1).cpu().numpy()
        cnts[ii] = (lab[:, 1:] != -100).sum(1).cpu().numpy()
    return sums, cnts


@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, tok, prompts, max_new, sample, seed):
    model.eval()
    texts = [tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": p}], tokenize=False,
                                     add_generation_prompt=True) for p in prompts]
    order = sorted(range(len(texts)), key=lambda i: -len(texts[i]))
    outs = [None] * len(texts)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    kw = (dict(do_sample=True, temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=0) if sample
          else dict(do_sample=False, temperature=None, top_p=None, top_k=None))
    for s in range(0, len(order), GEN_BATCH):
        ii = order[s:s + GEN_BATCH]
        b = tok([texts[i] for i in ii], return_tensors="pt", padding=True, add_special_tokens=False).to("cuda")
        with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            g = model.generate(**b, max_new_tokens=max_new, repetition_penalty=1.0,
                               pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id, **kw)
        for i, row in zip(ii, g[:, b["input_ids"].shape[1]:]):
            outs[i] = tok.decode(row, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
    return outs


def last_number(text):
    m = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text)
    return m[-1].replace(",", "").rstrip(".") if m else None


def task_eval(task, model, tok, test, seed):
    """Generation-based evaluation. Returns (metrics dict, per-item records)."""
    items = test[:C.N_GEN_TEST[task]]
    gens = generate(model, tok, [e["prompt"] for e in items], C.MAX_NEW_TOKENS[task],
                    sample=(task == "roc"), seed=777 + seed)
    if task == "mbpp":
        st = check_many([extract_code(g) for g in gens], [e["tests"] for e in items], [e["setup"] for e in items])
        return {"score": float(np.mean([s == "pass" for s in st]))}, [{"gen": g, "status": s} for g, s in zip(gens, st)]
    if task == "gsm8k":
        strict = [C.gsm_equal(C.gsm_extract(g), e["gold"]) for g, e in zip(gens, items)]
        lenient = [C.gsm_equal(C.gsm_extract(g) or last_number(g), e["gold"]) for g, e in zip(gens, items)]
        return ({"score": float(np.mean(strict)), "score_lenient": float(np.mean(lenient))},
                [{"gen": g, "correct": bool(c), "correct_lenient": bool(l)} for g, c, l in zip(gens, strict, lenient)])
    return {}, [{"gen": g} for g in gens]   # roc: generation metrics are computed in analysis


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- one run
def run(job, tok):
    task, cond, ratio, seed = job["task"], job["cond"], job["ratio"], job["seed"]
    t0 = time.time()
    torch.manual_seed(1000 * seed + 17)
    rng = random.Random(1000 * seed + 17)
    data = C.load_real(task)
    val_enc = [encode(tok, e) for e in data["val"]]
    test_enc = [encode(tok, e) for e in data["test"]]
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(C.STUDENT, torch_dtype=torch.float32).cuda()
    res = {**job, "key": job_key(job)}

    if cond != "zeroshot":
        train = C.train_set(task, seed, cond, ratio)
        enc = [encode(tok, e) for e in train]
        steps = max(math.ceil(EPOCHS * len(enc) / BATCH), MIN_STEPS)
        eval_at = {round(steps * (k + 1) / N_VAL_EVALS) for k in range(N_VAL_EVALS)}
        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY)
        warm = max(1, int(WARMUP_FRAC * steps))
        sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(
            opt, lambda s: (s + 1) / warm if s < warm else 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * (s - warm) / max(1, steps - warm))))
        step, best, best_state, curve, bl = 0, float("inf"), None, [], []
        while step < steps:
            for b in batches(enc, rng):
                model.train()
                ids, att, lab = (t.cuda() for t in collate([enc[i] for i in b], tok.pad_token_id))
                with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
                    loss = model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att, labels=lab).loss
                loss.backward()
                torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), GRAD_CLIP)
                opt.step(); sched.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
                step += 1
                if step in eval_at:
                    s_, c_ = nll_per_item(model, val_enc, tok.pad_token_id)
                    v = float(s_.sum() / c_.sum())
                    curve.append([step, v])
                    if v < best:
                        best, bl = v, step
                        best_state = {k: p.detach().clone() for k, p in model.state_dict().items()}
                if step >= steps:
                    break
        s_, c_ = nll_per_item(model, test_enc, tok.pad_token_id)
        res.update(n_train=len(enc), steps=steps, epochs=steps * BATCH / len(enc), best_step=bl,
                   val_curve=curve, val_nll=best, test_nll_final=float(s_.sum() / c_.sum()),
                   train_tokens=int(sum(len(e[0]) for e in enc)))
        model.load_state_dict(best_state)
        del best_state, opt
    else:
        s_, c_ = nll_per_item(model, val_enc, tok.pad_token_id)
        res.update(n_train=0, steps=0, val_nll=float(s_.sum() / c_.sum()))

    sums, cnts = nll_per_item(model, test_enc, tok.pad_token_id)
    res["test_nll"] = float(sums.sum() / cnts.sum())
    metrics, recs = task_eval(task, model, tok, data["test"], seed)
    res.update(metrics)
    res["seconds"] = round(time.time() - t0, 1)

    C.OUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with gzip.open(C.OUT_DIR / (res["key"].replace("|", "_") + ".json.gz"), "wt") as f:
        json.dump({"key": res["key"], "nll_sum": sums.tolist(), "n_tok": cnts.tolist(), "items": recs}, f)
    with open(C.RUNS_FILE, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(res) + "\n")
    del model
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return res


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--worker", type=int, default=0)
    ap.add_argument("--n_workers", type=int, default=1)
    ap.add_argument("--filter", default=".*", help="regex on job key task|cond|ratio|seed")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    torch.set_num_threads(4)
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(C.STUDENT)
    tok.padding_side = "left"
    jobs = [j for j in all_jobs() if re.search(args.filter, job_key(j))]
    jobs = [j for i, j in enumerate(jobs) if i % args.n_workers == args.worker]
    for j in jobs:
        done = {json.loads(l)["key"] for l in open(C.RUNS_FILE)} if C.RUNS_FILE.exists() else set()
        if job_key(j) in done:
            continue
        try:
            r = run(j, tok)
            print(f"[w{args.worker}] {r['key']}: n={r['n_train']} steps={r['steps']} val={r['val_nll']:.4f} "
                  f"test_nll={r['test_nll']:.4f} score={r.get('score')} {r['seconds']}s", flush=True)
        except Exception as e:   # log and continue; the job stays unfinished and can be retried
            import traceback
            print(f"[w{args.worker}] FAILED {job_key(j)}: {e!r}", flush=True)
            traceback.print_exc()
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/bin/bash
# Generate all synthetic pools with two teacher instances.
# Usage: run_generation.sh GPU_A GPU_B [GPU_FRAC]
# The GPUs are shared with other jobs, so each instance reserves only GPU_FRAC of the card and is
# restarted (generation is resumable) if it dies, e.g. from an out-of-memory error.
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && source .venv/bin/activate
export VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1   # system nvcc is too old for FlashInfer's JIT
FRAC=${3:-0.38}
NREQ=mbpp=7000,gsm8k=5200,roc=5200
launch () {  # gpu, jobs, logfile
  for try in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
    CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$1 python src/generate_synth.py --jobs $2 --n_requests $NREQ --gpu_frac $FRAC >> $3 2>&1 && return 0
    echo "[launcher] attempt $try failed on GPU $1; retrying in 60s" >> $3; sleep 60
  done; return 1
}
launch $1 gsm8k:0,roc:0,mbpp:0,gsm8k:2 logs/gen_A.log &
launch $2 gsm8k:1,roc:1,mbpp:1,roc:2,mbpp:2 logs/gen_B.log &
wait
EOF
rm -f logs/gen_seed*.log logs/gen_A.log logs/gen_B.log; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,memory.free --format=csv,noheader

"""E3: does the synthetic pool's diversity saturate as it grows (the hypothesised 'mode collapse')?

For nested prefixes of each synthetic pool, and for real data of the same size, compute
  * exact-duplicate rate of the task input (normalised text) and of a short "key" (title / function name),
  * near-duplicate rate: share of examples whose cosine similarity to an EARLIER example exceeds 0.9,
  * distinct-2: unique word bigrams / total bigrams, and the raw number of unique bigrams,
  * Vendi score (exp. entropy of the eigenvalues of the cosine-similarity kernel / n): an effective
    number of distinct examples,
  * coverage of the real test distribution: mean cosine similarity from each real test example to its
    nearest neighbour in the training prefix.
Embeddings: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on CPU. Output: results/diversity.json
"""
import json
import re
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np

import common as C

SIZES = [100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000]
NEAR_DUP = 0.9


def view(task, ex):
    """Text that characterises the *content* of an example (input side, plus the story for creative)."""
    if task == "mbpp":
        return ex["text"]
    if task == "gsm8k":
        return ex["question"]
    return ex["title"] + ". " + ex["story"]


def key(task, ex):
    """A coarse identity: function name / title / leading proper name of the word problem."""
    if task == "mbpp":
        m = re.search(r"def\s+(\w+)", ex["code"])
        return m.group(1) if m else ""
    if task == "roc":
        return ex["title"].lower().strip()
    m = re.search(r"\b([A-Z][a-z]+)\b", ex["question"])
    return m.group(1) if m else ""


def norm(t):
    return " ".join(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", t.lower()))


def vendi(E):
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh((E @ E.T).astype(np.float64) / len(E))
    ev = ev[ev > 1e-12]
    return float(np.exp(-(ev * np.log(ev)).sum()))


def stats(task, exs, E, E_test):
    out = {}
    texts = [norm(view(task, e)) for e in exs]
    keys = [key(task, e) for e in exs]
    S = E @ E.T
    prior_max = np.array([S[i, :i].max() if i else 0.0 for i in range(len(E))])   # similarity to any earlier item
    for n in SIZES:
        if n > len(exs):
            break
        bg = [b for t in texts[:n] for b in zip(t.split(), t.split()[1:])]
        kc = Counter(keys[:n])
        out[n] = {
            "exact_dup_rate": 1 - len(set(texts[:n])) / n,
            "key_dup_rate": 1 - len(kc) / n,
            "top10_key_share": sum(c for _, c in kc.most_common(10)) / n,
            "near_dup_rate": float((prior_max[:n] > NEAR_DUP).mean()),
            "distinct2": len(set(bg)) / max(1, len(bg)),
            "unique_bigrams": len(set(bg)),
            "vendi": vendi(E[:n]),
            "test_coverage": float((E_test @ E[:n].T).max(1).mean()),
        }
    return out


def main():
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    enc = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device="cpu")
    emb = lambda xs: enc.encode(xs, batch_size=256, normalize_embeddings=True, show_progress_bar=False)
    res, pool_info = {}, {}
    for task in C.TASKS:
        test = C.load_real(task)["test"]
        E_test = emb([view(task, e) for e in test])
        for seed in C.SEEDS:
            raw = C.load_pool(task, seed, only_valid=False)
            pool = [r for r in raw if r["valid"]]
            pool_info[f"{task}|{seed}"] = {
                "requests": len(raw), "parsed": sum(r["parsed"] for r in raw), "valid": len(pool),
                "exec": dict(Counter(r.get("exec") for r in raw if r.get("exec")))}
            pool = pool[:max(SIZES)]
            res[f"{task}|synth|{seed}"] = stats(task, pool, emb([view(task, e) for e in pool]), E_test)
            real = C.real_order(task, seed)[:max(SIZES)]
            res[f"{task}|real|{seed}"] = stats(task, real, emb([view(task, e) for e in real]), E_test)
            print(task, seed, "synth", res[f"{task}|synth|{seed}"].get(max(SIZES)) or list(res[f"{task}|synth|{seed}"].items())[-1])
            print(task, seed, "real ", list(res[f"{task}|real|{seed}"].items())[-1], flush=True)
            if seed == 0:   # most frequent keys: a direct look at the modes
                kc = Counter(key(task, e) for e in pool)
                pool_info[f"{task}|top_keys"] = kc.most_common(15)
    json.dump({"stats": res, "pools": pool_info}, open(C.ROOT / "results" / "diversity.json", "w"), indent=1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.thinking: I'll fix the NLL evaluation to compute loss only at answer positions instead of materializing full-vocabulary logits, and extend the MBPP pools to ~10.5k requests since the 3B teacher's lower code yield (~51% vs 77% for 7B) requires more volume to reach 5,000 usable examples.

input.command:
cd /data/summereunann/neurico-workspaces/the_synthetic_data_ceiling__di_20261012_130125_601c9c29 && source .venv/bin/activate && python - << 'EOF'
p='src/train_eval.py'; s=open(p).read()
old=s[s.index("def nll_per_item(model, enc, pad_id, bs=64):"):s.index("@torch.no_grad()\ndef generate(")]
new='''def nll_per_item(model, enc, pad_id, bs=32):
    """Summed NLL and token count of the reference answer for every item."""
    model.eval()
    order = sorted(range(len(enc)), key=lambda i: len(enc[i][0]))
    sums, cnts = np.zeros(len(enc)), np.zeros(len(enc))
    for s in range(0, len(order), bs):
        ii = order[s:s + bs]
        ids, att, lab = (t.cuda() for t in collate([enc[i] for i in ii], pad_id))
        with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            hid = model.model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=att).last_hidden_state
            tgt = lab[:, 1:]
            mask = tgt != -100
            # project only the answer positions onto the vocabulary (full-vocab logits for the whole
            # batch would cost several GB)
            logits = model.lm_head(hid[:, :-1][mask])
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.float(), tgt[mask], reduction="none")
        row = torch.nonzero(mask)[:, 0]
        sums[ii] = torch.zeros(len(ii), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float64).index_add_(0, row, loss.double()).cpu().numpy()
        cnts[ii] = mask.sum(1).cpu().numpy()
    return sums, cnts


'''
s=s.replace(old,new); open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
cat results/runs.jsonl 2>/dev/null | cut -c1-400; grep -h -E "^\[" logs/gen_*.log | tail -5; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.free --format=csv,noheader

"""Reference point: the teacher's own zero-shot score on the code and math test sets (same 500 items and
same scoring as the student), to document the teacher-student gap.

    CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=g python src/teacher_eval.py --gpu_frac 0.3
"""
import argparse
import json

import numpy as np

import common as C
from exec_eval import check_many, extract_code
from train_eval import last_number

HINT = {"mbpp": "", "gsm8k": "\nSolve step by step and end with a final line of the form '#### <number>'."}


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--gpu_frac", type=float, default=0.3)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
    llm = LLM(C.TEACHER, dtype="bfloat16", max_model_len=3072, gpu_memory_utilization=args.gpu_frac, seed=0)
    tok = llm.get_tokenizer()
    out = {"model": C.TEACHER}
    for task in ["mbpp", "gsm8k"]:
        items = C.load_real(task)["test"][:C.N_GEN_TEST[task]]
        prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": e["prompt"] + HINT[task]}],
                                           tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for e in items]
        gens = [o.outputs[0].text for o in llm.generate(prompts, SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=512),
                                                        use_tqdm=False)]
        if task == "mbpp":
            st = check_many([extract_code(g) for g in gens], [e["tests"] for e in items], [e["setup"] for e in items])
            out[task] = float(np.mean([s == "pass" for s in st]))
        else:
            out[task] = float(np.mean([C.gsm_equal(C.gsm_extract(g) or last_number(g), e["gold"])
                                       for g, e in zip(gens, items)]))
        print(task, out[task], flush=True)
    json.dump(out, open(C.ROOT / "results" / "teacher_baseline.json", "w"), indent=1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=g python src/teacher_eval.py --gpu_frac 0.3
"""
import argparse
import json

import numpy as np

import common as C
from exec_eval import check_many, extract_code
from train_eval import last_number

HINT = {"mbpp": "", "gsm8k": "\nSolve step by step and end with a final line of the form '#### <number>'."}


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--gpu_frac", type=float, default=0.3)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
    llm = LLM(C.TEACHER, dtype="bfloat16", max_model_len=3072, gpu_memory_utilization=args.gpu_frac, seed=0)
    tok = llm.get_tokenizer()
    out = {"model": C.TEACHER}
    for task in ["mbpp", "gsm8k"]:
        items = C.load_real(task)["test"][:C.N_GEN_TEST[task]]
        prompts = [tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": e["prompt"] + HINT[task]}],
                                           tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) for e in items]
        gens = [o.outputs[0].text for o in llm.generate(prompts, SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=512),
                                                        use_tqdm=False)]
        if task == "mbpp":
            st = check_many([extract_code(g) for g in gens], [e["tests"] for e in items], [e["setup"] for e in items])
            out[task] = float(np.mean([s == "pass" for s in st]))
        else:
            out[task] = float(np.mean([C.gsm_equal(C.gsm_extract(g) or last_number(g), e["gold"])
                                       for g, e in zip(gens, items)]))
        print(task, out[task], flush=True)
    json.dump(out, open(C.ROOT / "results" / "teacher_baseline.json", "w"), indent=1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-25919/bundled-skills/2.1.293/c505e548d094e98abdb5438cfafbc8ef/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
